A discontinued part number is a dead end only if the part number is all you have. The specification behind it usually is not dead.

" "

Start from the drawing, not the catalogue

Pull the original specification sheet or drawing: dimensions, ratings, materials, mounting, connectors and the environment the part works in. Those are what any replacement has to meet.

" "

Cross-reference against active and legacy lines

With the specification in hand, compare it against current manufacturer lines and against legacy stock still held in distribution. A match on the specification is a better answer than a near match on the part number.

" "

Know when to stop

If no available part meets the specification, keep searching only while the search is cheaper than the alternative. Past that point, reverse engineering a drop-in replacement from the original sample or drawing is usually faster than a redesign of the assembly around it.

" "

Send us the drawing or the old part number and we will tell you which of these you are in.

"), ("Why obsolete isn't the same as unavailable", "Obsolescence", "The four outcomes when a part goes out of production, and how to tell which one you are actually in.", "

When a manufacturer marks a part obsolete, buyers often assume it is gone. In practice there are four different situations, and each has a different answer.

" "

1. Still in the channel

The part is no longer made, but distribution and surplus stock still hold it. Buy what you need now, including spares.

" "

2. A successor exists

The manufacturer has a replacement. Check that it is a true drop-in: form, fit, function and any certifications the original carried.

" "

3. An equivalent exists elsewhere

Another manufacturer makes a part that meets the same specification. Confirm it against the drawing before it goes into a safety-critical system.

" "

4. Nothing exists

No successor and no equivalent. The part can often be reverse-engineered from the original sample or drawing.

" "

Tell us the part and we will tell you which situation you are in.

"), ("What a DBE certification actually unlocks on a transit bid", "Public Sector", "Supplier-diversity goals, counting rules, and what buyers need from you at pre-qualification.", "

Transit and airport contracts funded by the US Department of Transportation often carry a Disadvantaged Business Enterprise goal. A DBE certification is what lets a supplier's participation be considered against that goal.

" "

Certification and counting are separate

Holding a certification and having participation counted toward a goal are not the same thing. Counting follows the rules in force at the time of award, so prime contractors should confirm counting with the certifying program before relying on it.

" "

The 2025 reevaluation

The USDOT Interim Final Rule (49 CFR Parts 23 and 26, effective 3 October 2025) required existing DBE certifications to be reevaluated nationwide and suspended counting while reevaluation is incomplete. It did not revoke certifications.

" "

What buyers ask for at pre-qualification

Certification evidence, identifiers such as DUNS, UEI and CAGE, insurance certificates, and references. Globe keeps all of these on the Government page.
